summary: Updates the 6LoWPAN extensions to IPv6 Neighbor Discovery so a listener can subscribe to an IPv6 anycast or multicast address. It also updates RPL with a new Non-Storing multicast mode and support for anycast addresses.

eli5.summary: Tiny low-power gadgets can now sign up to hear group messages, like joining a mailing list, and the network knows where to send them.

subtitle: Lets tiny low-power IPv6 nodes subscribe to multicast and anycast addresses, and lets RPL routers carry those subscriptions.

tldr.problem: 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery only registers unicast addresses, so a battery-powered node had no way to tell its router which multicast or anycast addresses it listens to, and RPL had no procedure for the router to inject them.
tldr.mechanism: A new 2-bit P-Field in the registration option marks an address as unicast (0), multicast (1) or anycast (2), the router keeps one subscription per origin and injects the address into RPL once, and a new RPL Mode of Operation 5 does multicast by ingress replication in Non-Storing mode.
tldr.outcome: Constrained nodes can join multicast groups and anycast services through ordinary Neighbor Discovery messages without speaking RPL, though delivery over the lossy network is not guaranteed to be exactly once.

today: RFC 9685 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2024. It updates RFC 4861, RFC 6550, RFC 6553, RFC 8505 and RFC 9010, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Multicast Needs a Subscription Method
sections.content:
Low-Power and Lossy Networks (LLNs) are built to save energy, so nodes keep their radios off most of the time. Classic IPv6 Neighbor Discovery and Multicast Listener Discovery rely on multicast queries to all nodes, which does not fit nodes that sleep. RFC 6775 and RFC 8505 fixed this for unicast addresses by letting a node proactively register an address with its router using an Address Registration Option.

RPL (RFC 6550) can route multicast, but 6LoWPAN Neighbor Discovery registers only unicast addresses, and RFC 9010 says nothing about the router injecting multicast or anycast routes. RFC 9685 closes that gap: a 6LoWPAN Node (6LN) can subscribe the anycast and multicast addresses it listens to, and the 6LoWPAN Router (6LR) can inject them in RPL.

The RFC warns that delivery cannot be guaranteed once and only once over an unreliable network. Upper layer protocols must cope with duplicated or missing packets.
sections.eli5: Sleepy gadgets cannot keep shouting questions to everybody. So they quietly tell one helper which group messages they want, and the helper takes care of the rest.

sections.title: How Subscription Works
sections.content:
RFC 9685 extends RFC 8505 with a registration method called subscription for anycast and multicast addresses. A node registers unicast addresses it owns, but subscribes to multicast addresses it listens to. Unlike a unicast address, many parties may register the same address, and that is not treated as a duplicate.

The flow in the RFC: the node sends a Neighbor Solicitation with an Extended Address Registration Option, NS(EARO), to its 6LR. The router validates it with the 6LoWPAN Border Router (6LBR, the registrar) using an Extended Duplicate Address Request (EDAR) and Confirmation (EDAC), then replies with NA(EARO) and injects the route. The router keeps one registration per party but injects the route into the routing protocol only once per address.

When the R flag is set in a subscription, the 6LR injects anycast addresses and multicast addresses of scope larger than link-scope into RPL, using the longest subscription lifetime across the active subscriptions. A router that merges several advertisements becomes the new origin and uses its own Path Sequence and ROVR values.
sections.eli5: It is like many kids telling the same teacher they want the class newsletter. The teacher writes each name down but passes along only one request upward.

sections.title: The P-Field and Other Format Changes
sections.content:
The core format change is a 2-bit P-Field, the Registered Address Type Indicator. It is added to the EARO, to the flags of the EDAR message (which repurposes the old Status field) and to the RPL Target Option. Value 0 is unicast, 1 is multicast and 2 is anycast. Value 3 is intended for prefix registration, a later specification: in an RPL Target Option it is ignored and treated as 0, while in an EARO or EDAR the message must be dropped, optionally with status 12 "Invalid Registration".

With P-Field 1 and the R flag set, the 6LR joins the multicast stream. With P-Field 2 and R set, it injects the anycast address into the routing protocols it takes part in. RFC 4861 is also amended so that NS and NA messages may carry a multicast or anycast Target Address when used for a registration.

A new capability bit, the X flag at position 8 of the 6LoWPAN Capability Indication Option, tells a node that the router accepts unicast, multicast and anycast registrations.
sections.eli5: A tiny two-bit label on each sign-up says whether it is for one person, a whole group, or whichever helper is closest.

sections.title: RPL Changes: MOP 5 and Anycast
sections.content:
The RFC amends RPL (RFC 6550) in several ways. It mandates the ROVR field to identify the origin of a Target advertisement. The Path Sequence freshness comparison applies only between advertisements from the same origin, and a router that merges advertisements must advertise the longest remaining lifetime. When that lifetime expires it sends a no-path DAO with lifetime 0.

It adds Mode of Operation 5, Non-Storing with ingress replication multicast support. The DAO announces a multicast address as a Target, never as a Transit. The Root sends one copy of each multicast packet to every 6LR that is transit for the address, using the same source-routing header as a unicast packet for a leaf on that 6LR. For a Root-generated packet, only the last address in the header is multicast. For other packets, the Root encapsulates the multicast packet in a unicast outer header.

For anycast, a target is routed as anycast when the parent or Root has received at least one DAO with P-Field 2. When forwarding down, a router copies all children that advertised a multicast address, but for anycast it MUST copy one and only one child. Anycast applies to both addresses and prefixes.
sections.eli5: For group mail the boss sends one copy to each local helper, who hands it to the right gadgets. For anycast, only one of the willing helpers gets it.

sections.title: Refreshing State After a Reboot
sections.content:
A router that lost state, for example after a reboot, SHOULD send an asynchronous NA(EARO) with the new status 11, "Registration Refresh Request". A multicast version MUST go to the all-nodes link-scope address ff02::1, with the Target set to the link-local address the router previously exposed for registrations. The TID follows the lollipop rules: a TID below 128 must not be taken as a reboot.

The request may be repeated to improve the odds of delivery, with the TID incremented each time. By default the initial TID after boot is 252, the SEQUENCE_WINDOW is 4, the short period is 10 seconds, the retry interval is 1 second and the number of retries is 3. A receiving node must process one and only one request in a series.

The RFC also defines the Consistent Uptime Option (CUO), ND option type 42. It carries how long the sender has been up without losing state, a flag showing the sender is low-power, and a 12-bit Node State Sequence Information (NSSI) that changes when state the peer depends on has changed. A receiver that sees a newer boot time must reassess and reinstall any state it had installed in the sender.
sections.eli5: If a helper forgets everything after a nap, it shouts "please sign up again" a few times so every gadget hears it, and gadgets only answer once.

sections.title: Deployment and Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
Adding a new RPL Mode of Operation means a live network cannot be updated in place. The administrator creates a new RPL Instance with MOP 5 and lets nodes join it. In a green field where every node supports the RFC, a single instance can serve unicast, multicast and anycast. In a brown field with legacy devices, the RFC RECOMMENDS one instance for unicast, typically MOP 1, and a separate instance for multicast and anycast.

A mixed mode is also allowed, signaled as MOP 1 in DIO messages so legacy nodes can still join as leaves, if there are enough supporting 6LRs and the 6CIO signals support. A multicast address that spans a DODAG MUST use Realm-Local scope, and one that spans an RPL Instance MUST use Admin-Local scope.

Legacy nodes are handled gracefully. A legacy 6LR will not set the X flag, so upgraded nodes will not subscribe. A legacy 6LBR may report an anycast or multicast address as a duplicate in the EDAC, and the 6LR MUST ignore that status. In a MOP 3 instance, a multicast Target with P-Field 0 MUST be processed as if the P-Field were 1.
sections.eli5: New rules cannot be slipped into a running network, so you build a second network that uses them and move gadgets over, while old gadgets keep working in the old one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security sections of RFC 8505 and RFC 9010 also apply, and the link layer SHOULD be sufficiently protected against rogue access. Because subscription is done by Neighbor Discovery, an RPL-Unaware Leaf can obtain multicast delivery without being allowed to inject RPL messages, which bars a number of attack vectors from inside RPL.

Tracking the origin of a subscription is described as a first step toward a form of Route Ownership Validation in RPL. RFC 8928 protects unicast ownership with autoconfigured keys, but anycast and multicast addresses are not owned by one node. If RFC 8928 is used, a key pair MUST be associated with the address before deployment, the ROVR MUST be generated from it and installed in the 6LBR, and the key pair MUST be provisioned in every node that may subscribe.

How to distribute the ROVR values is out of scope. The RFC suggests authorizing the ROVRs of valid users in advance, and notes that updating the keys for an address across all nodes may not complete in time, so installing a new address may be simpler.
sections.eli5: Gadgets can ask to join a group through the helper, without being trusted to boss the whole network. A secret key can prove who is allowed to join.

sections.title: IANA Registry Changes
sections.content:
IANA created a new "P-Field Values" registry under ICMPv6 Parameters (value 3 unassigned) and an "EDAR Message Flags" registry in which bits 0-1 hold the P-Field. P-Field entries were also added at bits 2-3 of the Address Registration Option Flags and of the RPL Target Option Flags registries.

Other additions are RPL Mode of Operation 5, 6LoWPAN capability bit 8 (the X flag), Address Registration Option status values 11 (Registration Refresh Request) and 12 (Invalid Registration), and IPv6 Neighbor Discovery option type 42 for the Consistent Uptime Option.
sections.eli5: The official number book got new lines for each new label, status and option so every device uses the same numbers.
